claims.text: Adding approximately 1–3 wt% copper and applying a homogenization anneal will enhance the HEA's heat-transfer capability.
The copper addition will establish percolative conductive paths in the HEA.
The copper addition and anneal will preserve structural integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
The initial HEA has excellent mechanical strength and resilience.
The initial HEA has limited thermal conductivity because lattice distortion produces phonon scattering.
Homogenization annealing will ensure uniform distribution of the copper dopant.
The intervention is expected to function during thermal cycling and high mechanical loading at approximately 350–600 °C, conditions described as similar to reactor divertor service.
The treated alloy will have a homogenized microstructure containing continuous thermally conductive pathways.
Copper addition and homogenization will avoid unwanted phase separation and deleterious microstructural instability.
Copper has inherently high thermal conductivity.
Interconnected copper-rich conductive networks will reduce the HEA's overall phonon-scattering effects.
The annealing step will maintain phase stability.
The copper-doped HEA will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than current intermediate-layer materials.
The copper-doped HEA will retain high-temperature strength after the intervention.
The copper-doped HEA will retain creep resistance after the intervention.
Current HEA interlayers have robust mechanical properties but low thermal conductivity caused by lattice disorder.
Keeping the copper concentration low will avoid phase instability or detrimental secondary phases that would impair structural integrity.
Performance may vary with the specific HEA composition and processing history.
